en: Om. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa! May He—who is worshipped by the hosts of gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
who bestows the desired object upon people who possess devotion; and who is meditated upon by yogis who have abandoned all worldly aims—[grant success].

Worship the lotus feet of Yamāri, who bestows security; having bowed to the feet of the Guru, which grant the fulfillment of desires to practitioners, this *Mudrāprakāśa* is composed for the joy [of the seekers]. A *mudrā* is so called because it bestows (*rāti*) joy (*mudaṃ*)—that is, delight—to the gods. Thus it is said in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "The arrangement..."

Having understood this, one should display the mudrā during worship. Regarding this, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*: "It is called *mudrā* because it bestows joy (*muda*) upon the gods; 'that which bestows joy' is *mudrā*. Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere: "They produce joy for the gods and cause their minds to flow [toward them]; therefore they are called *mudrās*, and they should be displayed."
"O Kuleśvarī, she is to be shown"—the meaning is "she is to be displayed"; the word "at the time of worship" (pūjākāle) is the ellipsis;

the elision of the suffix *ṇi* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the tenth chapter of the *Gautamīya*, it is said that they are called *mudrās* by the wise because they cause delight (*modanāt*) to all the gods and because they cause the destruction (*drāvaṇāt*) of the succession of sins, thereby bringing about the presence (*sānnidhya*) of the deity.

Because it causes delight (*modana*) to all the gods and because it drives away (*drāvaṇa*) the succession of sins, this mudrā is therefore called *mudrā*, which accomplishes all desires and aims. According to the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "One who has not been initiated should not perform [this]; for the deities become agitated, and consequently the mudrās become fruitless."

He too would become diseased and poor. Regarding the mudrā called the goad (aṅkuśa) for the rite of invoking the sacred waters (tīrtha-āvāhana), its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "The practitioner of mantras should invoke the sacred waters with the mudrā in the form of a goad; the one called the goad consists of the right fist with the index finger made into a hook."

In the fourth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava* it is said: "Having formed a fist with the left hand, the index finger in the form of a goad is called the 'Goad' (*Aṅkuśa*) mudrā; it becomes the attractor of the three worlds. For protection, the 'Spear' (*Kunta*) mudrā is taught; its characteristic is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: the two fists with the thumbs raised, the index..."
"One should place the *nyagrodha* [fig tree]—for this is proclaimed as the *kunta-mudrā*, which provides all protection.
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the *kumbha-mudrā*, its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
"Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb, if one forms a fist with both hands leaving a space in the middle, [that is the *kumbha-mudrā*]."

This mudrā is called Kuṃbhā; it is described as having a central space and being empty in the middle. In that same section on bathing, it is stated: "In the consecration with the Kuṃbha-mudrā, one should place the right thumb into the left fist, while the other fingers of that [left] fist remain at its side, leaving an internal space.
Thus, the fingers of the right hand, excluding the thumb, are within the fist.

Those going toward the left and those at the side of the left fist—[pointing to] that left fist, which is the intermediate space, empty in the middle—in the seventh chapter of the Gautamīya, it is said: "One should encircle the fist made with the left hand with the right hand;
this shall be the mudrā called Kalaśa, auspicious and the remover of all sins. In that interval, [the right...]
Having placed the right thumb into the left thumb and formed a single fist with both hands leaving a space, that is the *kuṃbha-mudrā*.
When the left thumb is placed upon the right thumb, leaving a space in the middle so that it is hollow, it is called by the name *tattva*;
this mudrā, which consists of the joining of the thumbs and ring fingers, is prescribed for many ritual acts.

Thus it is said in the thirteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*: "This is declared to be the *Tattvamudrā* by means of the thumb and the ring finger. The *Kālakarṇī* [mudrā] is to be employed in rites for the pacification of obstacles;
its characteristic, as stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*, is described as follows: having formed two fists with the thumbs raised upwards...

One should form the *Kālakarṇikā* mudrā, which destroys obstacles, by bringing the two joined fists face-to-face; likewise, in the *Tantrasāra* it is said: "Having raised the two thumbs while the two fists are joined together, one should turn those very [thumbs] toward each other—this is the *Kālakarṇikā* mudrā."

The definition of that [mudrā] for the meditation on the one named Vāsudeva is likewise given in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "The *añjali* joined with the middle and ring fingers is the *vāsudevāhvayā* (named Vāsudeva) mudrā; and that same *añjali* [is used], with the elision of the case-ending as is common in poetic usage (*chāndasaḥ*). Now, the mudrās for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* [are described] in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "With the middle and ring fingers... [and so forth].
On the forehead, the middle fingers are placed; on the eyes, the head, lips, hands, joints, and sides, the ring fingers are used;
on the ears, the index and middle fingers;
on the nose, the index and little fingers; on the cheeks and mouth, three middle fingers; on the teeth and tongue, three ring fingers; and on the back, three [fingers].

The *niṣṭhā* letters (*kha*, *gha*, *cha*, *jha*, *ṭha*, *ḍha*, *tha*, *dha*, *pha*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*) together with the long vowels (*vṛddhi*) are likewise assigned to the navel; all [the remaining letters] are said to be in the stomach.

The *tala* [letters] are said to be in the heart and other locations. The placement (*nyāsa*) performed with these *mātṛkā-mudrās* bestows the fruit [of the practice]. In another *tantra*: "One should place the ring finger and middle finger on the forehead for the sake of the face; the index finger..."

Placing the ring fingers on the two eyes, the thumbs on the two ears, the little fingers and thumbs on the two nostrils, the three middle fingers on the two cheeks, the middle fingers on the two lips, the ring fingers on the two teeth, the middle fingers on the head, and the ring fingers on the mouth— The provided text consists of instructions for a ritual placement of fingers (mudrā) upon various parts of the body. Here is the translation: Place the ring fingers on the two eyes, the thumbs on the two ears, the little fingers and thumbs on the two nostrils, the three middle fingers on the two cheeks, the middle fingers on the two lips, the ring fingers on the two teeth, the middle fingers on the head, and the ring fingers on the mouth.

One should place the middle fingers on the hands, feet, and sides; the little, ring, and middle fingers should be placed on the back. All those [fingers], together with the thumbs, should be placed at the navel region and on the belly. One should place the entire palm on the heart, on both shoulders, and on the region of the back; [likewise] on the heart, first the hands, feet, and belly.
The palms [of the hands] are likewise placed upon the faces; these mudrās of the Mothers have been proclaimed in their proper order.

For one who performs the nyāsa without knowing them, that nyāsa shall be fruitless. In the phrase "the middle finger with the mouth," the word "mouth" (mukha) refers to the tongue; thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Therefore, it is said: [vyo...]

Regarding the phrase "menddhaurasanārṇakarṇikam" and so forth, by the word *aurasana*, the visarga is understood. However, this point must be noted here: the term *pārśvayoḥ* (of the two sides) is connected only with *kaniṣṭhā-anāmikā-madhyā* (the little finger, ring finger, and middle finger), and not with the *madhyamā* (middle finger).

Otherwise, by the statement "one should place [the fingers] when asked," the word *tā* (those) would result in redundancy. Furthermore, what was stated by the author of the *Mantradarpaṇa*—namely, that the middle finger (*madhyamā*) is [placed] on the head, the lips, the hands, the joints, and the sides—is to be considered; for the tips of the fingers have not been mentioned.

And because of that, it should be understood that what was stated by the author of the *Mantradarpaṇa* is to be contemplated. Now, regarding the *aṅganyāsa* and *mudrās*, the *Mantradarpaṇa* says: "The heart is said to be formed with three [fingers], the eye with two; the weapon (*astra*) and the head (*śiras*) are likewise considered [to be formed with two];
the topknot (*śikhā*) is known to be formed with the thumb, and the armor (*kavaca*) is declared to be formed with the [remaining] fingers. With the [remaining] fingers...
With ten [fingers], the wise one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart using the middle, ring, and index fingers;
he should perform the placement on the head with the middle and index fingers; on the tuft (*śikhā*) with the thumb;
he should place the armor (*kavaca*) with ten [fingers]; and the weapon (*astra*) should be on the eyes with three [fingers].
These are known as the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) when directed upward from the middle and index fingers.

In the *Yāmala*, the heart is said to be formed by the middle, ring, and index fingers; the head by the middle and index fingers; and the topknot (śikhā) by the thumb and [the other fingers]. With all ten [fingers]...

Speech is said to be formed with three fingers; the eye is declared to be formed with two fingers; the weapon (astra) is formed with [the remaining] two fingers—this is considered the arrangement of the limbs (*aṅga-kalpanā*).
With the three fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers are assigned respectively to the three eyes. If it is the eye...

The author of the *Tantrasāra* states that "two [fingers] are prescribed there, namely the index and the middle," based on a citation from Bhaṭṭa; thus, regarding the *astra-mudrā*, there is a specific distinction made with the two aforementioned fingers—the middle and the index—according to the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "between the index and middle fingers of the right hand."
One should cast [the hand] with the left thumb extended; by the striking [of the fingers], there shall be sound. This is declared as the *astramudrā*.

Regarding the specific procedure for the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], it is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "At the heart and the head, the four fingers [are joined] excluding the thumbs; at the armor (*varman*), they are straight; and at the weapon (*śiras*), it is a fist with the thumb extended."

Facing downward, with the two hands raised and the thumbs and index fingers joined at the tips while making a sound, this is the Astra-mudrā of Viṣṇu; it is used for the eyes. For Narasiṃha, the middle finger of the right hand [is used], and likewise for the other [deity] according to the *Tantrasāra*: "The fingers, excluding the thumb, are straight."
The mudrās are formed with the fingers of the hands at the heart and the head;
at the crest-lock (śikhā), it is a fist with the thumbs pointing downward; for the armor (varman), the fingers of both hands should be joined;
and the sound of the nārāca-mudrā arises when the two arms are raised and the thumbs and index fingers are extended.
The weapon-mudrā (astramudrā) is described as being like a dog's [paw]; where there are two eyes, there the index finger and middle finger are placed.

After the words "where there are two eyes," the word "there" (tatra) is to be supplied; thus, the meaning is this: where there are two eyes, i.e., the pair of eyes, there the index and middle fingers are to be placed upon the altar (vedi).

The meaning is that this applies to other Viṣṇu-mantras, excluding the Narasiṃha; however, since Narasiṃha has three eyes, the aforementioned mudrā—consisting of the three fingers beginning with the index finger—is to be understood as the placement for his eyes. Others, however, maintain that all the *tattva*-placements (*nyāsa*) should be performed.

Likewise, in the third chapter of the Gautamīya Tantra, it is said: "O Sage, one should perform the nyāsas with the mind alone, or with a flower; otherwise, if performed with the thumb and ring finger, it becomes fruitless. Thus [is described] the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā, which severs the tip of the tongue of the enemy.
Hāṃ! Likewise, at the time of performing the placement (nyāsa) concerning the Śrīvidyā, the wise one should demonstrate it accordingly;

and thus, in the twelfth chapter of the Jñānārṇava: "Or else, O Great Goddess, [perform] the supreme placement of the Śrīvidyā; one should contemplate the complete Vidyā, possessing an orange luster, in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). SRA.
One should meditate upon the sixteen-syllable mantra that bestows great good fortune; then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī on the region of the left shoulder.

One should place the mudrā that seizes the tongues of enemies at the base of the foot. Having said this, the collection of placements (*nyāsajāla*) has been described; now follows the definition of these two.

As it is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "Having formed a fist with the left hand and keeping the index finger straight, one should whirl it around the left ear; this is the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā during nyāsa. Having completely restrained the three worlds with the fist inside which the thumb is placed, [one should place it] on the sole of the left foot."
Regarding the placement of the Āsāri-yujihvāgra-hā-mudrā, it is stated in the twelfth chapter of the Jñānārṇava: "The best of mantra-knowers,
having formed a fist with the left hand at the region of the ear and extending the index finger straight,
should rotate it at the time of the placement of the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī-mudrā."

Having suppressed this earth with the fist formed by the thumb and the other fingers as indicated, at the time of performing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ripujihvāgrahā* mudrā, it is indicated in another tantra: "One should place the *ripujihvāgrahā* mudrā upon the sole of the left foot. Thus, these two mudrās [are described] in the latter half [of the verse]. The right...
"It is not drunk with the hand," such is the view; and likewise in another Tantra:

"The right fist with the thumb tucked inside, resembling the grasping of an enemy's tongue, with the index finger straightened—this is the Mudrā Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī. Having formed the fist with the right hand, the thumb being hidden within—"

"One should place [the mudrā] on the tip of the tongue, the head, and the sole of the left foot"—here, the word "these" (*etān*) is to be supplied as the object of the action. These words are cited by the author of the *Mantradarpaṇa* in the section on the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *Śrīvidyā*; they refer to the deity known as Kūrmamudrā.
Regarding the ritual of meditation (*dhyānakarman*), its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
"On the left [hand], at the ancestral (*pitṛ*) tīrtha, the thumb and the fourth finger [are joined]; on the right [hand], the middle and ring fingers face downward;
the index finger is slightly bent; the other three fingers of the left [hand] and all those of the right [hand] have their faces turned upward on the back."
Having placed the right hand with the thumb raised, resembling the back of a tortoise, one should meditate;

this is known as the *kacchapa-mudrā*. Then, one should join the middle and ring fingers of the right hand, facing downwards, between the index finger and thumb of the left hand. Furthermore, [the same applies to] that left [hand].

One should place the right thumb between the middle finger and the index finger (tarjanī); then, the small finger (kaniṣṭhā) of the right hand should be placed upon the index finger of the left hand. The remaining three fingers—the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger—should have their tips pointing upward and be joined to the back of the right hand. This is stated again for the right [hand].

The meaning is that one should form the palm of the right hand like the back of a tortoise by making the thumb [of the left hand] so positioned. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: one should join the little finger of the right hand with the index finger of the left hand, and likewise join the left thumb with the right index finger; the right [thumb] should be raised.
One should join the middle and other fingers of the left hand to the back of the right hand;
likewise, with the middle and ring fingers of the left hand according to the *pitṛ-tīrtha*,
one should place them facing downward upon the back of the right hand, making it level with the shell of a tortoise.

One should place the right hand on all sides; this is declared to be the *kūrmamudrā* for the practice of meditating upon the deity. The author of the *Tantrasāra* states that it is formed by placing [the hands] on the back and the chest. The definition of this mudrā in the meditation on the three-sectioned *Tripurā* is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "The two [hands] are joined together..."
One should form a circle with the middle fingers joined and the little fingers straight.
When the ring fingers are bent inward by the two index fingers, this is the *trikhaṇḍā* [mudrā]. Furthermore, in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*:

"Having turned the hands over, one should make the two thumbs touch each other evenly; having placed the ring fingers inside, [the index fingers... (the text continues with the formation of the *trikhaṇḍā*).
O Maheśvarī, one should join the two little fingers, which are curved at their tips, in their respective places;

this is known as the *trikhaṇḍā* [mudrā] for the practice of meditation on Tripura. Furthermore, in the twelfth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, O Maheśānī, it is said that by means of the rotation of both hands...
Having joined them, O Beloved, one should hold [the hands] with the two index fingers touching;
the middle fingers should be joined at their centers, and likewise the ring fingers below them.
Having also joined the thumbs in a threefold manner according to the sequence of pairs, this is the mudrā named Trikhaṇḍā, which destroys enemies.
Regarding the *bhakāriṇī* [mudrā], one should move the *gālinī* mudrā back and forth over the half-moon; its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
"Having placed back upon back and joined the two thumbs with the two little fingers, one should form the others [as follows]..."
This is the *gālinī* seal described by Ralā; it is also taught elsewhere:

when the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined together, and the index, middle, and ring fingers are held closely together and curved [toward the palm], this seal is called *gālinī*, used for purifying water from a conch shell.

In the ninth chapter of the *Gautamīya*, it is stated that one should recite the root mantra of Gālinī ten times and place it upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Having extended the two hands toward each other in the manner of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*), one should employ the right thumb with the left little finger, and likewise the left thumb [with the right little finger].

This is considered the Kṣiṇayā mudrā, known as the Aṅgālinī; it is said to bestow the fruit of the *arghya* when moved above the mouth. With the *śikhā* [mudrā] and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, using the right little finger, one should [hold] the *arghya* vessel with the mudrā called Matsya.
The wise one should cover [the left hand]; its definition is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
"Having placed the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand, one should properly move the two thumbs to form the mudrā in the form of a fish. It is also stated elsewhere:
One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand and properly press the two thumbs together;
this is the Matsyarūpiṇī mudrā. This mudrā has been declared by the wise to be for the invocation of the deity; it is called Āvāhanī (invoking) and Sthāpanī (establishing).
The third is the *sannidhāpanī*, the fourth is the *sannirodhanī*, the fifth is the *sanmukhīkaraṇī*, the sixth is the *sakalīkaraṇī*, the seventh is the *avaguṇṭhanī*,
the eighth is said to be the *amṛtīkaraṇī*, which is the *dhenumudrā*, and the ninth is the *paramīkaraṇī* mudrā.
The ninth [mudrā] has been proclaimed; the characteristics of these others have been declared in sequence in the *Mantradarpaṇa*:

having raised the hollowed palms upward, one should then place them downward; that which is described as the *āvāhanī* (invocation) becomes the *sthāpanī* (installation) when turned face-downward. These two...

The meaning is "three times two turns. When the pair of fists is embraced with the thumbs pointing upward, it is for the purpose of *sannidhāna* (invocation). This mudrā, containing the thumbs within, is renowned as being for *sannirodha* (confinement).
For [in that case], the two fists are made with the palms facing upward; this is for *saṃmukhīkaraṇa* (making present), O God.

The placement of the *ḍaṃ* syllable (*ḍaṃganyāsa*) is here declared to be the act of complete protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*). If the left hand forms a fist with the index finger straightened and pointing downward, it is the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*. When this [mudrā] is rotated all around from the *kavaca* [mantra], it is performed in a counter-clockwise direction (leftward rotation).

The meaning is that one should recite the *kavaca* (armor) mantra and so forth in sequence, ending with *iti kavacam*. This mudrā, consisting of the syllable *huṃ*, is also formed with both hands; this will become clear from the subsequent statements in the *Gautamīya-tantra* and the *Jñānārṇava-tantra*. [The two hands] are joined together.

The *gomudrā* is described by Varuṇa as follows: with the thumbs and forefingers slightly bent and the middle fingers joined, one should consecrate [the offering] with nectar using the Varuṇa seed-mantra, "vaṃ. In this mudrā, the two thumbs are interlaced and the other fingers are extended.

One should make the fingers of the opposite hand supreme; this is called the *mahāmudrā* by the poets in the tenth chapter of the *Gautamīya*. One should turn the raised *añjali* downward; this becomes the *āvahaṇī*. This same mudrā, when reversed, is the *sthāpanī*.

"Not inverted in action" means facing downwards. When the two outer thumbs are joined, it is the *muṣṭīmudrā*, which is the *sannidhāpanī* (invoking presence). That same mudrā, with the thumbs placed inside [the fists], is the *sannirodhanī* (confining). With both fists turned upward, it is the *āsammukhīkaraṇī* (making face-to-face).
The *avaguṇṭhanī* [mudrā] is considered to be formed by the rotation of a pair of index fingers toward one another;
"toward one another" means preceded by moving toward each other,
and thus, from the right index finger, it is performed by turning clockwise onto the left index finger.
The realized meaning is that by rotating [the hands] counter-clockwise, the *Avaguṇṭhanī-mudrā* is formed.

In that very context: having joined the fingers of the left and right hands together, the right ring finger is joined with the left little finger, and the left ring finger is joined with the right little finger.
The knuckle of the right hand's little finger should be pressed by the right middle finger;

the left hand's index finger should be pressed by the left middle finger; and the two index fingers should be joined together. A wise person should touch both thumbs as well; this is declared to be the Dhenu-mudrā, which is kept secret.
O sinless one, in the fourth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, [the Lord] spoke of the mudrās beginning with the *āvāhanī* (invoking gesture): "One should turn the raised *añjali* downwards;
this becomes the *āvāhanī*. Here, the term *añjali* refers to the two thumbs placed upon the root joints of the ring fingers."

One should join the palms in *añjali* with the fingers interlaced (*yasaṃyoga-yuktām*), as this is consistent with the statements of other tantras to be cited hereafter that hold the essence of the tantra; the same should be understood for the two previously mentioned statements as well. However, if it were the reverse, it would become the *vaiṣṭhāpanī* [mudrā], which consists of two joined fists.
The form of *sannidhāpana* consists of the two thumbs; the form of *sannirodhana* consists of the two thumbs being held between the fists.

Here, because of the mention of "between the thumbs" (*antar-aṅguṣṭha*) and for the sake of consistency with other scriptural statements, it is understood that in the preceding mudrā, the two thumbs were on the outside of the pair of fists.

When the two index fingers of this very mudrā are straightened, it is the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, which accomplishes all tasks. The phrase "the two index fingers are straightened" implies that they are rotated around [the head], as understood from other statements and the unity of the sentence; these are the limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantra*).
The best of practitioners should place [the mantras] upon the limbs of the Goddess; this is the mudrā called *sakalīkaraṇa*, which consists of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Regarding the phrase "upon the limbs of the Goddess," here the word "Goddess" (*devī*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); O Dear One, having joined [the hands] together in one place during the performance of the *ārātrika* rite, it is called *paramīkaraṇa*.
Beyond that, this mudrā is like the *ārātrika* (the waving of lights), meaning it is shaped like a triangle;
if the reading is *ārātrikavidhau*, the meaning is that it has the form of a triangle.
Then, having performed the rotation, the little finger and the ring finger are joined with the index and middle fingers.
Joining the two hands together is declared to be the *dhenumudrā*, which effects the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
In the *Tantrasāra*, it is stated that having formed an *añjali* with both hands, one should place the two thumbs upon the root joints of the ring fingers; this is known as the *āvāhanī mudrā*.
If this [mudrā] is turned face downwards, it is known as the *sthāpanī* (establishing) mudrā.
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, it is the *sannidhāpanī* (invoking presence).
That same [mudrā], with the thumbs inserted inside, is considered the *saṃrodhanī* (confining). [The one] with both fists turned upwards...
The placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the deities for the purpose of acceptance is known as *sakalīkṛti*.
This is the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, formed with the left hand into a fist with the index finger extended and pointing downward;
it is considered to be rotated all around with the fingers facing one another.
Furthermore, when the little finger and ring finger are joined together, and likewise the index and middle fingers, it is proclaimed as the *dhenu-mudrā*.
By means of this, the best of practitioners should perform the consecration (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
When the thumbs are interlaced and the other fingers are extended, this is declared to be the *mahāmudrā*.
The wise should employ this mudrā for the purpose of bringing about the supreme state and in the rite of summoning the deity.
The Lelihānā mudrā, however, is proclaimed for the placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa).
Its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "They should be facing downwards..."
One should make the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger short and straight;

having cast out the extended ring finger, this is prescribed as the *jīvanyāsa* (life-depositing) mudrā, which is called *ālelihā*. In the *Tantrasāra*, it is stated that the index, middle, and ring fingers are [short].

One should not make [the fingers] face downward; one should place the ring finger on the little finger, straightening it and licking it—this is proclaimed as the *jīvanī* mudrā for the placement of life-force (*jīvanyāsa*).
Now, regarding the mudrās for incense and other offerings, in the *Tantrasāra* and in another tantra: [the middle and ring fingers...]
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the tips of the thumb and ring finger while reciting the root mantra;

he should present flowers to the wheel with the thumb and forefinger. O Goddess, the wise should offer incense in the same manner as the fragrance, using the middle and ring fingers for the central part.

O Lord of Devas, holding the incense with the tip of the thumb, the preceptor of the ritual should offer it. Having performed the upward movement (*uttolana*) and placed [the vessel], he should offer the food (*naivedya*) to the God while reciting the Gāyatrī and the root mantra, using the *tattvāśu* mudrā. He should then give water for sipping (*ācamana*) and betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) with the root mantra.
In the thirteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said regarding the offering of flowers with the *tattva-mudrā*:

"O Goddess, one should offer the flower with the mudrā known as *jñāna*. The *jñāna-mudrā* is proclaimed to be formed by joining the thumb and index finger. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) with the *prāṇa* and other mudrās, [one should proceed].
The wise one should demonstrate their forms as follows:

touching the little finger and the ring finger with the thumb is the *prāṇa-mudrā*; touching the ring finger and the middle finger with the thumb is the *apāna-mudrā*; [touching] the middle finger, the index finger, and the thumb... [is the *vyāna-mudrā*].
One should touch [the heart] with the thumb, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger; this is the Vyāna-mudrā.
One should touch [the throat] with the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and ring finger; this is the Udāna-mudrā. One should touch the four fingers, beginning with the index finger, to the thumb;
this is the Samāna-mudrā. Thus it is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa* regarding the worship of Kālī.

In the section on waking, one should touch two fingers at a time in direct order (anuloma) by releasing each preceding finger starting from the little finger (kaniṣṭhā), and in reverse order (viloma) by touching three or four fingers; as stated in the *Bālāvilāsatantra*:
"The little finger (kaniṣṭhā), the ring finger (anāmikā), the ring finger, the middle finger (madhyamā), and the middle finger, [then] the forefinger (tarjanī)."

One should touch the three fingers beginning with the index finger (tarjanī) and the fourth (the middle finger) with the thumb in succession. These are the Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna breaths; they are preceded by the syllable *Tārā* (Oṃ), followed by *Dviṭha* (Sva) at the end. O Dear One, these mantras for the breaths and so forth, beginning with *Oṃ*, are the mudrās from the east onwards. The mantras for the breaths and so forth begin with "Oṃ Prāṇāya Svāhā" and so on.

The meaning is that the mudrās of prāṇa and so forth are those described by the sequence beginning with "trāḥ, the little finger and the ring finger" and ending with "ityādinākramāt. The prāṇa-mudrā is as before; alternatively, one should touch the middle finger and the index finger with the thumb—this is the apāna-mudrā; [and] the ring finger and the middle finger...

One should touch with the thumb; this is the Vyāna-mudrā. The Udāna-mudrā and the Samāna-mudrā are likewise as before. Furthermore, in the Mantracintāmaṇi it is said: "One should touch the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger with the thumb; [then] the ring finger and the middle finger—these three."

"The four beginning with the index finger"—thus [the phrase] "beginning with the index finger" (*tarjanyādyāḥ*) is connected to both [sides] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). The word "four" (*catasṛkāḥ*) refers to those joined with the letter *ṛ*, as in some instances even a preceding vowel may be heavy due to its association with *ṛ*. These are the mudrās of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are accepted in the *Svatantra-tantra*.

There is no violation of the meter here, as in the following example: "Who are you? "A dwarf Brahmin. "What do you want? "The sacrificial fee for this king's sacrifice. "Take gold, a cow, and land measured by three paces;
I request these from you. While Bali was saying this, [Vāmana grew].
May Vāmana, whose form strides across the three worlds with three steps and who has a smiling face, protect you.
Furthermore, in the *Kramadīpikā*: "One should touch the little finger and the ring finger to the tips of one's own thumbs; this is the first hand-gesture (*mudrā*). Likewise, [the second].
The first [mudrā] consists of the middle fingers;

the second consists of the ring and middle fingers; the third consists of the ring, index, and middle fingers; likewise, the fourth consists of those same fingers plus the little finger; and the fifth is declared to be similar to that.

The mantras of the path of Kṛṣṇa consist of the mudrās of Prāṇa and the others, joined with their respective mantras—Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna—each in turn joined with the dative case-ending and preceded by the *tārā* (the syllable Om). If these are bound as supports for the *tārā*, they are the supports of the *tārā* belonging to the path of Kṛṣṇa; that is, they begin with the *praṇava*.

The fires, kindled by the *vadhū* and *svāhā*, are beautified at the end; such is the remainder [of the sense]. Thus, one should display the mudrās of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth in sequence, while reciting the five mantras beginning with "Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā. In the *Yāmala*, the *grāsa-mudrā* is also mentioned.

The fingers, curved and with their tips closely joined, placed together in the right hand, are known as the Grasamudrā. Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna are to be known as the five vital breaths (prāṇas).
The five breaths, joined with the thumb, the little finger, and the ring finger,
are known as the *prāṇa-mudrā* for the rite of offering to the vital breath (*prāṇāhavana*).
If the index, middle, and thumb fingers are joined together as one, it is the *apāna-mudrā*.
The *nāhutī-mudrā* is formed when the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb are joined together;

this *yuktā-vyāna-mudrā* is prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homaka*). That *mudrā* which is performed without the little finger is known as the *dāna-havana*. When all [fingers] are employed, it is remembered as the *samānā-huti-mudrā*.

These fourteen statements regarding ritual action (*karma*) are cited from the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī* in the fourteenth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the work titled *Mudrāprakāśa*, composed by Rāmakiśora. Thus ends the section concerning the determination of common mudrās and so forth.
The mudrās of Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Sun, Gaṇeśa, and Ambikā are also described there;
however, the ten mudrās of Śiva are as follows: the Liṅga, Yoni, that called Triśūla, the Māleṣṭā, the one named Bhṛga, the Khaḍga, the Gā, the one called Kapāla, and likewise the Ḍamaru.
Now, the characteristics of these [mudrās] are described in sequence from the *Mantradarpaṇa*:
one should bind the raised right thumb with the left thumb;
then, one should bind the left fingers with the right fingers—this shall be the *liṅga*.
The meaning of "liṅgamudrā" is as follows: having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers dexterous, one should join the two ring fingers at the back of the middle fingers;
then, one should employ the two little fingers by means of the curved inner parts of the index fingers.

When the middle finger is placed in the hollow of the palm and the little fingers are positioned like fire, and the two thumbs are extended, then if one extends these three [fingers] while binding the little finger with the thumb—
this is declared to be the Triśūla mudrā, held in the right hand.
Having joined the tips of the index finger and the thumb, one should extend the other three fingers together;
this is called the *akṣamālā* (rosary) mudrā by the poets.
For the *varadābhaya* (granting boons and fearlessness) mudrā, one should form hands like those granting boons and fearlessness, with all the fingers straightened.

Having placed the thumb at the base of the index finger, one should apply the tips of the middle and ring fingers to the head of the little finger; this shall be the *mṛga-mudrā*. For the remaining [fingers], one should raise them all together; the five fingers of the right hand should be joined and raised halfway.

Having made the left hand like a vessel, placing it upon the body, and raising it as if it were a skull-bowl, one should perform the mudrā known as Khaṭvāṅga; this is said to be dear to Śiva. Having made the right fist loose, [this is the procedure].

One should move it slightly when raised toward the ear; indeed, this is the *ḍamarumudrā* according to the *Tantrasāra*. One should bind the raised right thumb with the left thumb, and bind the left fingers with the right fingers. [The *liṅga*...]

This is declared to be the *gamudrā*, which brings about the presence of Śiva: having interlocked the little fingers with one another, and having placed the two index fingers over the two ring fingers, and beneath the two long middle fingers joined at their tips, one should place the two tips of the thumbs; this is the *yonimudrā*.
Having bound the little finger with the thumb and extended the three remaining fingers joined together,

this is proclaimed as the mudrā named Triśūla (Trident). Having formed a knot at the tips of the thumb and the index finger and extending the three [other] fingers, this is proclaimed as the Akṣamālā (Rosary) mudrā.

The right hand placed below with the fingers extended is the *vara-mudrā* (boon-granting gesture); the left hand raised above with both hands extended is the *ubhaya-mudrā*; the palm turned downward with fingers extended is the *nikubja-prasṛti*, as Amara states: "the palm turned downward with fingers extended is *nikubja-prasṛti*"; and the thumb joined with the tips of the middle fingers is [the *tarjany-aṅkuśa-mudrā*].

One should join them; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā* (deer-mudrā), characterized by the fingers being joined and raised. Regarding the phrase "joined and raised" (*śliṣṭāṅgulyucchrite*), there is no grammatical irregularity here due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). As for the *khaṭvāṅgamudrā*: the five fingers of the right hand are joined together and raised halfway.

The *drāvi* mudrā is considered very dear to the Lord; having placed the left hand like a vessel and likewise upon the left shoulder, one should raise it upward— this is known as the *kāpālikī* mudrā, formed by making a loose fist.
Raising the middle finger six units, one should move the right hand upward toward the region of the upper ear;
this mudrā, the *ḍamaruka*, destroys all obstacles.
These [instructions] were maintained by the author of the *Tantrasāra*; prior to meditation, one should perform this worship with these mudrās.
One should display these; in this same manner, other deities should also be understood by practitioners.

Thus it is said in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "Having displayed the mudrās and performed the binding of the directions (digbandha), one should meditate upon the Lord of the Universe. Furthermore, the author of the *Tantrasāra* has also [described] the placement (*nyāsa*) in the ritual manual for general worship (*sāmānyapūjāpaddhati*).

Having removed the net (jāla), then having displayed the various mudrās prescribed in the respective Kalpas, performed meditation, and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch; this is stated in the Sanatkumāra Tantra as well: "The worship of the pedestal, the sacrifice to the limb-deities, and the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) [should be performed] in that manner."
"In this world, invocation, the fashioning of one's own seal (mudrā), meditation on the Lord, and worship—these constitute the five-fold initiation.

This was cited by the author of the *Tantrasāra* in the section on the five-fold initiation (*pañcāyatanadīkṣā*). Furthermore, in the twelfth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, after describing the network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*), it says: "Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the rule..."
Having stated, "O you whose body is armored with the forest-mudrās," and having commenced by saying, "The nine mudrās known as Kṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādanī, Mahākuśā, Khecarī, Bījā,
and Yonī follow in sequence," and having described those respective mudrās, [it continues]: "Thus, having arranged the body..."

Having stated that "one whose body is bound by the six mudrās should perform the rite of internal sacrifice (antaryāga), for by that he is himself directly the Lord," the twelfth chapter is concluded. Then, in the thirteenth chapter,
after describing meditation, the rite of internal sacrifice is taught, including the display of mudrās at the conclusion of the worship.

It is stated in that very same [text], and likewise in the tenth chapter of the *Gautamīya*: "Having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should display the mudrās in sequence. At the conclusion of the worship:
"I bow to Kṛṣṇa in the form of a cowherd, the delight of the cowherdesses, whose eyes are like fresh blue lotuses and who resembles a fresh rain-cloud."
Having uttered the praise beginning with "ṇamaḥ" and so forth, and having then displayed the mudrās, one should perform the consecration of the fire (agnisaṃskāra); this is what has been stated.
According to the maxim that "the meaning of the scripture established in one place [applies] everywhere," the common applicability of this rule should be understood. Thus says Nārāmakiśora Dvijāti.

In this second chapter, titled "The Determination of Mudrās," composed within the *Nāmamudrāprakāśa*, this concludes; it is that which is constantly meditated upon by the lords of ascetics for the sake of easily crossing the ocean of saṃsāra,
and which is worthy of worship by the hosts of gods.

Worship Mukunda, who holds a lotus, a conch, a discus, a mace, and a flute, and who possesses the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; O virtuous ones, worship Him! The wise have declared nineteen mudrās of Viṣṇu:
the conch, discus, mace, lotus, flute, Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, vanamālā (garland), as well as the jñāna-mudrā, bilva, and the hand gesture of the arm.

The mudrā called Rūḍhā, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu; likewise the Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Hayagrīvī, Dhanus, Bāṇa, Paraśu, and the supreme Jaganmohinikā; these are known as the Kāma-mudrās—their characteristics shall indeed be described hereafter.
In the *Traddarpaṇa*, there are nineteen mudrās of Viṣṇu, beginning with the conch, discus, mace, and club.

Holding the left thumb with the right fist, one should extend [the fingers] while making a hollow [fist]; both fists should be joined at the tips, and the fingers of the left hand extended so that they touch the right thumb. This should be performed.
If the thumb and little finger are joined and bent while the others are extended, this is the conch mudrā (śaṅkha-mudrā).
Having brought the two hands together facing each other, this is the wheel mudrā (cakra-mudrā).
One should bring the two hands together with their palms touching and the fingers interlaced; this is declared to be the mace mudrā (gadā-mudrā).

When the hands are joined and extended at the middle, this is the Padma-mudrā; if the two hands are brought face-to-face, the fingers should be joined at the palms with the thumbs depressed and raised,
the left thumb touching the right little finger and the right [thumb] touching the left [little finger].

The wise person should make the little finger straight against the back of the right thumb; having slightly contracted the remaining three fingers, one should move the flute. This is characterized by the form of the *ṛti* [mudrā], where the back of the right thumb is joined [to the flute]; because of the occasional weightiness of the preceding [syllable], there is no metrical defect (*chando-bhaṅga*) here.

The remaining fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers—are called the *veṇu* (flute); this is the meaning of the *veṇu-mudrā*. Having placed each finger against its corresponding one on the back, one should bind the two index fingers with the little finger, and likewise bind the middle and ring fingers together with the thumb; such is the arrangement of the *vipra* [mudrā].
This is known as the Śrīvatsa mudrā:

having joined the right little finger to the back of the ring finger, one binds it with the left little finger; the right ring finger and middle finger are placed upon the thumb, while the other fingers are straightened.

It should be understood that all four fingers of the left hand are joined at the tips as described for the *stubha-mudrā*, while those of the right hand are joined with the middle finger; this constitutes the two [mudrās]. By joining the index and thumb fingers from the neck down to the feet of both hands, there arises the *vanamālā-mudrā*.

Like a garland, by touching the tips of the index finger and thumb joined together, one should place [the hand] at the heart according to the rite; or, the left hand placed on the left knee is the mudrā named Jñāna.
Holding the upward-pointing tip of the left thumb with the right thumb, the remaining fingers likewise touch its tip.
Furthermore, O one of pure Vaiṣṇava intellect, having firmly bound [the hands] with the fingers and recalled Smara (Kāma), one should establish this Gopī-vilva-mudrā in the heart;
it consists of the seed-syllable of Smara (klīm), with the two hands turned away, the two index fingers and the two little fingers [joined].
With the two thumbs joined together and the middle and ring fingers likewise [joined] as wings, one should move them according to the prescribed rite;
this is declared by the wise to be the Gāruḍa-mudrā.
Having placed the hands between the knees with the palms touching the ground, one should repeatedly shake the face and open the mouth and the region of the chin.

One should perform the *saṃlelihāna* mudrā by licking [the lips]; the one called *nṛsiṃha* is formed by pressing the two thumbs or the two little fingers together with all the fingers facing downward; this is the mudrā of the god Nṛhari, which is held above him.

Having made oneself prone, one should bend the hands downward; this is the Vārāhī mudrā, which the mantrin should show to him. With the right and left hands facing upward and downward respectively, with the tips of the fingers joined, it is known as the Vārāhī mudrā. [The right hand] upon the palm of the left hand...

The secret mudrā (gulya) should be formed by placing the fingers facing downwards; having raised the neck of the horse [of the hand], one should bend the middle fingers downwards. Having bound the left ring finger and little finger with the thumb, one should display the bow joined to the tips of the middle and index fingers upon the left shoulder. This is the *yojya* [mudrā].
Thus, the meaning of "the bow-mudrā" (*dhanurmudrā*) is the specific positioning of the middle and index fingers;
having formed a fist with the right hand, one should join the extended middle and index fingers between them,
pull them back, and touch the ear— this is the mudrā of Śakti and Viṣṇu.

The mudrā called pivāṇa is said to be the same as the śara-mudrā; however, from the previously described right fist, one should extend the index finger straight, join the palms of both hands together horizontally, and make the other fingers closed and extended— this is declared to be the paraśu-mudrā.
Having formed two fists with the two thumbs pointing upward— this is the "Mohanī" (deluding) mudrā for the worlds—

and having joined the two hands so that the fingers are extended and the two index fingers are positioned on the back of the middle fingers while the two thumbs rest in the hollow of the middle fingers; this is the meaning of the "Kāmamudrā," known as Kāma and Kāminī.
In another tantra it is said: "Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist, one should then turn the fist upward and extend the thumb.
Likewise, the fingers of the left hand, joined and extended, should be touched by the right thumb."

Having joined the middle finger with the base of the thumb and keeping the other four fingers straight and touching the fire [the ring finger], this mudrā known as Kaustubha should be applied from the throat down to the feet; likewise, with both hands like a rosary, one should touch with the index finger and thumb.
Placing the tips of the index finger and thumb together, one should position them at the heart;

the left lotus-hand should be placed upon the top of the left knee. This is known as the Jñānamudrā, which is the beloved of Lord Rāmacandra. The left thumb should be raised upright, while the other [fingers] are...

Having grasped the tip of it with the thumb and pressed it with the fingers, and having bound it firmly with the fingers of the left hand, one of pure intellect should place it upon the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra; this is clearly described here as the mudrā known as Bilva. Go!
By those skilled in the ritual of the beverage, with the thumb of the other hand [the left],
one should press the thumb of the right hand; then, with the fingers of that right hand—
that is, the fingers of the right hand— one should [visualize] the *mā* seed-syllable and the *kāma* seed-syllable upon the hands.
Having turned the two hands away from each other and interlaced them at the little fingers,
with the two index fingers joined together and the two thumbs likewise joined, one should move the two middle and ring fingers like wings;
this shall be the Garuḍa-mudrā of Viṣṇu, which increases his satisfaction.
Placing both hands between the knees with the palms turned upward and the fingers touching the ground, trembling again and again, one should turn the face back and lick the tongue;
this is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases that [power]. The method is as follows.

Placing the two thumbs between the palms and likewise joining the two little fingers, with all other fingers facing downward—this is considered the mudrā of Nṛhari. Placing the left hand above the deity, palm upward, the wise one should bend it downward; this is proclaimed as the mudrā known as Vārāha. Thus it is explained.

The *mudrā* known as Vārāhī is formed by placing the right hand facing upward and the left hand facing downward with their fingertips joined together. Alternatively, having placed the fingers of the right hand face-downward upon the palm of the left hand, one should bend the middle finger down and hook it.
Moreover, this [mudrā] is dear to Hayagrīva and imitates his form:
one should join the middle and index fingers at their tips on the left side;
one should press the ring and little fingers against it with the thumb; and one should display it over the left shoulder—this is declared to be the bow mudrā (dhanurmudrā).
Alternatively, the arrow-seal (*bāṇamudrikā*) consists of the clenched fist with the index finger extended. Or, as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Dear One, make the hand like a bow held in the hand;
this is declared to be the bow-seal (*cāpamudrā*), situated on the left hand, just as arrows are held in the hand."
O beloved, perform the *thāhasta* [gesture]; this is declared to be the *bāṇamudrā*, which cuts down the host of enemies.
Having joined the fingers of both hands together and then spread them out sideways, one should form the mudrā known as *paraśu* (the axe). [Then] raise the thumb...

The *muṣṭidvaya-mudrā* is the *trailokyamohinī*. Having joined the two hands with the fingers extended, the two index fingers [are placed] on the backs of the middle fingers, and the two thumbs rest upon the middle fingers; this is the celebrated *kāma-mudrā*, which is dear to all the gods. These [are the mudrās].

The following mudrās, cited from authoritative sources by the author of the Tantrasāra, are to be employed in the worship of the respective deities: for the worship of Śrī Gopāla, one should employ the Veṇu-mudrā;

for the worship of Nṛhari, the Nārasiṃhikā; and for the worship of Vārāha, one should employ the mudrā known as Vārāhī. In the worship of Hayagrīva, one should display the Hayagrīvī mudrā. Rā... [text fragment]

In this chapter on the *mudrās* composed with effort by the twice-born Nārāyaṇa Kiśora under the name Mudrāprakāśa, during the worship of Paraśurāma— known as the *mārcana*, *dhanuḥ*, *bāṇa*, *mudrā*, *paraśu*, and *jaganmohana*— this is the *peṃdra-mudrā*.

The third chapter, titled "The Final Decision," is concluded. One should worship that Sun-like Lord, the ocean of compassion and sovereign of the three worlds; by worshipping Him, the multitude of sins perishes just as darkness vanishes at sunrise.
This alone is proclaimed to be the defining characteristic of a lotus among men. Thus [ends the section].
To that Gaṇeśa, whom the gods led by Śakra praise as the Sun of the virtuous, and at whose mere remembrance all obstacles swiftly dissolve— Gaṇeśa who possesses the seven mudrās known as the tusk,
the noose, and the goad, as well as those called the obstacle-destroying axe and the like.

Those known as *ḍukasaṃjñikā* and *bījapurāhvayā* have their characteristics described in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "The right fist turned upward, with the middle finger straight and its tip pointing upwards—
this is declared to be the *Gaṇeśamudrā*, which grants joy."

Having formed two fists and joined the left index finger with the right index finger, if one places the tips of those two [index fingers] at the tips of the thumbs, it is a "noose" (pāśa). If one should cast the two tips of the thumbs against the tips of the index fingers, it is a "noose"; this is the meaning of the *pāśamudrā*. Thus it is performed.

When the middle finger is straight and the index finger is joined at its middle joint and bent slightly, it is the beautiful *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. When the same [fingers] are turned downward, it is called the *rada-mudrā*; that very same [mudrā] is proclaimed as the *vighna-mudrā*, while the *paraśu-mudrā* is described [as follows].

One should form the hand gesture known as the *laḍḍuka-dāḍima-mudrā* (the seal of the sweetmeat and pomegranate). According to the *Tantrasāra*: "The *daṃtamudrā* (tooth-seal) is described by those skilled in all its aspects as being with the middle finger raised upward, straight, and the fist closed. Furthermore, [one should place] the index finger of the left fist upon the right fist...
Having joined the two index fingers, one should insert the tips of the two thumbs into the tips of the two index fingers;
this is proclaimed by the wise as the mudrā called Pāśa (the Noose).
Then, having made the middle finger straight and joining the index finger at its middle joint, one should bend it.
Among these, the mudrā known as the goad (*aṅkuśa*) consists of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers with the thumb in a fist, turned downward and elongated in form;
the middle finger [extended] is the obstacle-averting mudrā (*vighnamudrikā*); and the axe-mudrā (*paraśumudrā*) is well-known as the *laḍḍu*.

The *mudrikā* known as *bījapūra* has been omitted here because it is already well-established; this determination of the *mudrās* for recitation (*paricchedibhāṣya*) has been composed with great effort by the twice-born Nārāmakiśora in his work titled *Mudrāprakāśa*.

The fourth [chapter] is named "Nāmagata": Rāma-kiśora— frightened, wretched, devoid of devotion, and fallen at the feet of her whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, the daughter of the mountain king, who possesses the noose, goad, and boon, and who is the light of compassion— desires [her grace].

The Bhīti, Khaḍga, Carma, Dhanus, Śara, Mauśalī, Daurgī, and Mahāyonī—these are the beloved mudrās of Śakti; their characteristics are now declared: the noose (pāśa), goad (aṅkuśa), boon-granting gesture (vara), fear-dispelling gesture (abhīti), bow (dhanus), and arrow (bāṇa) are thus described.
Regarding the characteristics of the sword-mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*), according to the *Mantradarpaṇa*, if one forms it with the right hand for those of small stature,
it becomes the sword-mudrā when the middle finger touches the straight [index finger] while the thumb is joined with the ring and little fingers;
likewise, in another tantra, the ring and little fingers are bound by the thumb.

When the remaining fingers are extended from the thumb and joined at the back, it is the sword-mudrā (*khaḍga-mudrā*). Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the shield-mudrā (*carma-mudrā*), the *Mantradarpaṇa* states: "Having placed the left hand in that same manner, one should extend it afterwards with the fingers slightly curved."

The leather-mudrā (carma-mudrā) should be as follows; it is also described in another tantra: having likewise extended the left hand sideways and made its fingers curved, this is declared to be the leather-mudrā.
Now, the characteristics of the pestle-mudrā (muśala-mudrā) and the Durgā-mudrā [are as follows].
Just as in the *Maṃtradarpaṇa*, if one forms fists above, below, right, and left,
then from those [fists] arises the mudrā called the *muśala*; if this same [mudrā] is placed upon the head,
it is the primordial *muśala-mudrā*, beloved by Durgā, the destroyer of obstacles, and the foremost of its kind.

In the *Tantrasāra*, having formed fists with both hands, one should place the right hand over the left; this is the *muśala-mudrā*, which destroys all obstacles. Having formed fists with both hands and placed the right over the left, one should join them to the head.

This is declared to be the Daurgī-mudrā. Now, regarding the characteristics of the Mahāyoni-mudrā, as stated in the Mantradarpaṇa: having brought the two hands together facing each other, one should form a bond with the two index fingers; the middle fingers should be placed back-to-back and extended, while the little fingers are joined at their bases in the hollow; this is called the Yoni-mudrā, [the thumb being... the thumb.

When the two index fingers are placed at the tips [of the thumbs], the two middle fingers in the middle, and the two little fingers in the hollow of the palms; when the two middle fingers are in the hollow of the palms and the tips of the two little fingers are joined at their two tips; and when the two thumbs are at the bases [of the little fingers]—this indeed is the *yoni* and the *mahāyoni*.
When the thumb is placed in the middle of its [the *yoni*'s] inverted interior, it becomes the *bhūtinī*. This is its [the *bhūtinī*'s] nature.

Then, for those two little fingers, the source (*yoni*) should likewise be the great source (*mahāyoni*). Within that source, which is curved and crooked, and joined with the thumb (*sāṅguṣṭa*), one should join the index, ring, middle,
and little fingers in their respective order from both hands, as stated in the *Tantrasāra*.
Having placed the tips of the thumbs at the base of the root [of the ring fingers], it is proclaimed as the "Great Yoni" (mahāyoni).

The two index fingers should be joined with the two ring fingers; the middle finger should be joined with the middle finger; and the little fingers, positioned in the lap [of the hands], should likewise have their bases joined.

The meaning is that when the two tips of the thumbs are placed [there], it becomes the *mahāyoni*. Another method is described in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: having joined the hands in the hollowed-palm gesture (*puṭita*), the tip of one's own thumb at the base of the little finger constitutes the *yoni* and the other [thumb] the *parayoni*; this mudrā is known as the "Beloved of Kālī."

It is also declared in another Tantra: having formed the hollow of the hands like a casket and joining the tip of the thumb to the base of the little finger, it is called the *aparayoni* (the other womb). This is the *muṇḍamudrā*, the beloved of Kālī; its characteristic is stated in the *Mantradarpaṇa*: "But the fist..."
One should place the thumb inside the left hand and join the tip of the thumb to the index finger which is attached to the tip of the right middle finger;
joining the right hand in this manner as a fist and displaying it on the right side is known as the *mastakamudrā* of Kālī.
In the *Tantrasāra*, having formed a fist with the left hand by placing the thumb inside... [the middle finger].
